reference.source: Apley & Solomon / standard sports medicine references
clinicalPearls: Pain localises to the medial epicondyle and the origin of the wrist flexor-pronator group, aggravated by resisted wrist flexion and forearm pronation
Like its lateral counterpart, it is a degenerative tendinopathy of the common flexor origin rather than a true inflammatory epicondylitis
It is much less common than tennis elbow and is linked to gripping, throwing, and pronation-loading activities
The ulnar nerve lies immediately behind the medial epicondyle and can be irritated or entrapped alongside the tendinopathy
Examination shows tenderness over or just distal to the medial epicondyle with reproduction of pain on resisted wrist flexion
Always assess ulnar nerve function and check for a positive Tinel sign at the cubital tunnel, as concurrent ulnar neuropathy alters management
Management mirrors lateral epicondylitis, centred on load reduction and a progressive eccentric flexor-pronator strengthening programme
Steroid injection carries the added risk of ulnar nerve injury and offers only short-term benefit, so it is used cautiously
Consider valgus overload and medial collateral ligament pathology in throwing athletes with medial elbow pain
reference.pathophysiology: Golfer's elbow is an overuse tendinopathy of the common flexor-pronator origin at the medial epicondyle, particularly involving pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis. Repetitive flexion, pronation, and valgus loading cause microtrauma and a failed healing response, producing mucoid degeneration and disorganised collagen. Proximity to the ulnar nerve means concurrent nerve irritation is common.
additionalDifferentials: Ulnar nerve entrapment at the cubital tunnel
Medial collateral (ulnar collateral) ligament sprain or valgus instability
Cervical radiculopathy referring to the medial forearm
Little Leaguer's elbow (medial apophysitis) in skeletally immature athletes
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound to confirm flexor-pronator tendinopathy or tearing
MRI to assess the tendon and the medial collateral ligament in refractory or athletic cases
Nerve conduction studies if ulnar neuropathy is suspected
Plain radiographs or stress views if bony injury or valgus instability is considered
redFlags: Progressive ulnar nerve symptoms with weakness or intrinsic hand muscle wasting
Night pain, systemic features, or a mass suggesting infection or tumour
Significant trauma or instability raising concern for ligament rupture
Persistent symptoms despite appropriate rehabilitation prompting diagnostic review
reference.prognosis: Most patients improve with load management and progressive strengthening, though recovery may take months; coexisting ulnar neuropathy or valgus instability tends to worsen outcomes and may need specific treatment.
pitfalls: Missing associated ulnar nerve entrapment, which can dominate the clinical picture
Injecting corticosteroid without regard to the closely applied ulnar nerve
Failing to recognise medial collateral ligament injury in throwing athletes
Treating as inflammatory with rest rather than addressing the tendinopathy with loading
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
